reviewHtml:
At today’s show, Marie Adam-Leenaerdt turned a darkly lit room into the suggestion of a supermarket, complete with refrigerators stocked with fruits and vegetables. It was a supermarket in spirit only, and certainly not in dress code. The idea of grocery shopping took a rather strange turn: Black lace became a see-through apron dress; ballooned shorts, held out around the hips, passed for a skirt; and a fascinator hovered somewhere between funeral etiquette and the confidence of a very self-possessed wedding guest. For the finale, a model emerged swathed in red fabric like a human red carpet. The groceries, clearly, were beside the point.

The joke was intentional. For her eighth collection, Adam-Leenaerdt was thinking about the kind of clothes that make you feel immediately well dressed, prompted by a customer who told her on Instagram that putting on one of her trench coats had exactly that effect. Her ambition was to make le chic sufficiently easy so you could wear it to the supermarket, in the garden, or anywhere else life happens to take you. Ideally without dropping the tomatoes while pushing a shopping cart matching your outfit.

A floating chiffon dress had the domesticity of a housewife and the attitude of a nightclubber. A wire structure kept the waist of a miniskirt in a strange, perfectly circular orbit around the hips. Balloon skirts turned out to be shorts, revealing one leg equipped with a garter belt; slit skirt-trousers did something similar with considerably less commitment. A sexy bodysuit came attached to a draped dress. Quilted jackets borrowed the padded proportions of old shopping bags. Taffeta was deployed in colors that usually turn up at weddings and thankfully nowhere else, then twisted into clothes that felt considerably less ceremonial.

Leenaerdt’s Belgian sensibility kept the practicality from becoming worthy. Everything had a slight twist, a small structural oddity, a perverse element of “why not?” The clothes were functional but never behaved themselves entirely. The supermarket, then, was less a literal setting than a fantasy of everyday life in which getting dressed is taken seriously but not solemnly. No special occasion required; no elaborate justification necessary. You can wear the lace apron, the sculptural skirt, the taffeta—even the carpet—if the mood strikes you. And if someone asks why you are dressed like that to buy broccoli, Adam-Leenaerdt’s answer seems to be: Why aren’t you?
